section_summary: This section combines FBI reports, State Department memoranda, and Navy transmittals concerning suspected Japanese espionage, political activity, and propaganda in the United States. Its largest group of documents consists of David Warren Ryder’s proposals for influencing American opinion about Japan through publications, lectures, radio, films, and trade arguments. It also includes a 1938 letter defending Japan’s position in China, a lecture itinerary, and a proposal that continues beyond page 63.

subfiles.title: FBI covering letter transmitting communications
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards communications for State Department information.
subfiles.summary: Forwards attached communications.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Miss Lauritsen
subfiles.from: John G. Gr…; FBI Los Angeles office
subfiles.about: An FBI inquiry examines allegations that a civilian evacuee from Manila collaborated with Japanese forces.
subfiles.summary: An informant alleges Miss Lauritsen traded with or assisted Japanese forces during the occupation of Manila. She denies the allegations, describes the seizure of her factory, and supplies her background and destination.

subfiles.title: American Legation transmittal of Schoen letter
subfiles.about: The legation forwards a letter addressed to the Emperor of Japan and suggests investigating its writer.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Schoen’s letter and envelopes; questions his mental balance.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Emperor of Japan
subfiles.about: Schoen offers a brief religious blessing for the emperor and Japanese people.
subfiles.summary: Offers a religious blessing for the emperor and his people.

subfiles.title: Japanese Counter-Intelligence Data, number 3
subfiles.from: William A. Carr, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards listed reports on Japanese organizations, firms, banks, and suspected espionage.
subfiles.summary: Lists counterintelligence enclosures sent in response to Carroll’s request.

subfiles.title: Foreign Activity Correlation working note
subfiles.about: A fragmentary handwritten note appears to outline political-party characteristics and history.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary outline of political parties, including platforms, personalities, and history.

subfiles.title: Japanese Counter-Intelligence Data, number 2
subfiles.from: Frederick Welden, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards a memorandum listing translations intended for the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a translation list; says the documents will follow separately.

subfiles.title: E 1/S translations to be forwarded to State Department
subfiles.about: The memorandum enumerates translations on Japanese government, military, labor, and social institutions.
subfiles.summary: Lists 31 translations selected for forwarding, including materials on Japanese ministries, police, industry, student mobilization, and armed forces.

subfiles.title: Japanese Counter-Intelligence Data, number 4
subfiles.from: William A. Carr, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: The Navy transmits a report on former U.S. residents suspected of Japanese espionage or propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a report on suspect Japanese formerly active in the United States.

subfiles.title: Mikhail Nicholas Gorin and Hafis Salich
subfiles.from: State Department Division of Eastern European Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum reconstructs a 1938 espionage prosecution and Gorin’s 1941 release and deportation.
subfiles.summary: Chronicles the arrests, convictions, appeal, proposed exchange for two Americans imprisoned in the Soviet Union, and Gorin’s departure after the State Department requested his release.

subfiles.title: FBI covering letter transmitting report
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon; Chief of Naval Intelligence; Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2
subfiles.about: Hoover distributes an attached FBI communication concerning Japanese-American political activity.
subfiles.summary: Forwards an FBI report to State, Navy, and Army intelligence recipients.

subfiles.title: FBI report on the Japanese-American Committee for Democracy in Cleveland
subfiles.about: The FBI investigates the Cleveland committee’s membership, meetings, officers, and reported Communist contacts.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates roughly 30 members and describes meetings, social events, officers, and a left-wing outlook. It compiles interviews, publication references, and informant allegations concerning contacts with Communist Party members and labor activists; several names are heavily degraded by OCR.

subfiles.title: Documents concerning David Warren Ryder and Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Okami identifies Ryder’s apparent work for the Japanese consulate and lists supporting documents.
subfiles.summary: Okami describes Ryder’s proposed publicity agency, substantial campaign budgets, and possible connection with Ralph Townsend. The memorandum asks whether Ryder registered as a Japanese agent and inventories twelve supporting items.

subfiles.title: Copy of memorandum on David Warren Ryder
subfiles.about: This is a duplicate copy of Okami’s memorandum and enclosure list on Ryder.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates the memorandum on Ryder’s propaganda work and its list of supporting documents; copied pages appear out of sequence.

subfiles.title: Educational Campaign: Special Plan
subfiles.about: A proposed Pacific Coast publicity campaign budgets nearly $500,000 for press, film, lectures, pamphlets, and radio.
subfiles.summary: The plan centers operations in San Francisco and estimates annual costs of $499,850. It proposes a weekly news bulletin, placed articles, educational films, lectures, two monthly pamphlets, and 52 radio broadcasts. Its explanations stress credible information, broad distribution, and an indirect approach to public influence.

subfiles.title: Letter to Roy W. Howard
subfiles.about: Ryder criticizes Scripps-Howard’s treatment of Japan and argues against American involvement in the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Ryder contends that unfavorable coverage of Japan encourages an American war scare and overlooks Soviet interests in China. He challenges collective-security arguments, invokes the Versailles settlement and the Kellogg-Briand Pact, and quotes John Bassett Moore and Edwin M. Borchard. He urges Howard to present Japan’s position and avoid rhetoric that could build support for war.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on discreet methods of improving Japanese-American relations
subfiles.about: Ryder recommends a gradual, quiet campaign that advances Japan’s interests through trade and anti-Communist arguments.
subfiles.summary: Ryder proposes initially avoiding conspicuous advocacy for Japan. He suggests press and lecture material criticizing Russia, Britain, and China, promoting American nonintervention and Japanese trade, and presenting Japan as a barrier to Communism. He favors developing the campaign gradually as opportunities emerge.

subfiles.title: Report of lecture tour by Alfred Katz
subfiles.about: A table records California lectures presenting arguments favorable to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lists venues, topics, and audiences for lectures from November through April.

subfiles.title: Supplemental Memorandum Concerning Special Campaign of Education (Political Only)
subfiles.about: A nationwide political publicity proposal outlines a news bureau, publications, and lectures to improve Japan’s image.
subfiles.summary: The proposal places headquarters in San Francisco and calls for weekly bulletins, monthly pamphlets, newspaper and magazine articles, and a lecture bureau. It describes intended audiences, possible bureau names, staffing, distribution, and an estimated annual cost of $205,790. The materials are meant to shape American understanding of Japan’s policies.

subfiles.title: A Rough Outline of Proposals Concerning the Improvement of American-Japanese Relations
subfiles.about: Ryder proposes a sustained campaign to reverse unfavorable American opinion of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ryder argues that Americans misunderstand Japan’s conflict with China and its relationship with Russia. He recommends subtle, gradual publicity centered on trade and opposition to Communism, carried out in an American style. The visible pages outline a news bureau, a monthly digest, radio talks, and motion pictures; the proposal continues beyond page 63.
